Use the following commit messages to make sure your assignment progress is transparent at any time:

if you have begun the task, but it is not yet meaningfully complete (less than ~30% of the task is done)

title: 3  Introduction to Node.js
text:
3.5 Hello World
Create the file hello-world.js with the following content:
console.log("Hello World!");
Afterwards open the directory of hello-world.js in a terminal and type the following command:
$ node hello-world.js
As output you will get:
> Hello World!
Please note: You don’t have to type the $ and you won’t get a > in the output. These prefixes should just help you distinguish between terminal inputs and outputs. To make it clear, you have to type node hello-world.js and you will get Hello World! as the output.
In the future we will shorten the description of such an example like this:
$ node hello-world.js
> Hello World!

4.3 Project dependencies
The following problems have to be solved in every project that depends on libraries:

How do we define which dependencies the application needs?
How do we know if dependencies should be updated?
How do we reinstall dependencies on another machine?

npm solves those problems with the file package.json.

title: 4  Introduction to npm
text:
4.4 Create a package.json

Open the project directory in your terminal.
Run the following command:
$ npm init
As a result, a file called package.json will be created:
{
  "name": "npm-demo",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1"
  },
  "author": "John Snow",
  "license": "ISC"
}

title: 4  Introduction to npm
text:
4.5 Install the chalk package

chalk is a package for formatting your console output.
You can install it via npm:
$ npm install chalk


💡 The exact version depends on the current npm registry. At the time this material was updated, the latest release is 6.0.0, so the version shown below may differ slightly in your environment.


You can check the installed chalk version:
$ npm list
> npm-demo@1.0.0 /home/mh/node/npm-demo
> └── chalk@6.0.0
You will also find a new dependency in package.json:
{
  "name": "npm-demo",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "",
  "main": "index.js",
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1"
  },
  "author": "John Snow",
  "license": "ISC",
  "dependencies": {
    "chalk": "^6.0.0"
  }
}

4.6 Semantic versioning

Version number format: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
6.0.0 means

MAJOR = 6
MINOR = 0
PATCH = 0

Increment:

MAJOR when you make incompatible API changes
MINOR when you add functionality in a backwards compatible way
PATCH when you make backwards compatible bug fixes

More details: semver.org

title: 5  Introduction to TypeScript
text:
5.1 Why TypeScript?
You have written JavaScript before, for plain web pages. This chapter is about what TypeScript adds on top of it, and about the handful of rules that decide whether the type system helps you or gets in your way.
JavaScript is dynamically typed. A variable can hold anything, and a typo in a property name is only discovered when that line of code actually runs — possibly in production.
TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript: every valid JavaScript program is a valid TypeScript program. It adds a type system that is checked before the program runs.
Everything you already know about JavaScript still applies. What you add is the description of what the values are — and that description is gone again by the time the program runs.

title: 5  Introduction to TypeScript
5  Introduction to TypeScript
section: 5.2 The most important sentence of this unit
text:
5.2 The most important sentence of this unit

Types exist at compile time only. At runtime there is nothing left but JavaScript.

TypeScript is transpiled to JavaScript, and during that step all type information is erased. There is no typeof check against your interfaces, no reflection, no casting that verifies anything.
const data = JSON.parse(text) as Article;   // compiles fine
console.log(data.price.toFixed(2));         // crashes if the JSON had no price
This matters enormously as soon as data enters the program from outside — a file, an HTTP request, a database. You have to validate it yourself. We will do this in every exercise of this unit.

title: 5  Introduction to TypeScript
section: 5.3 Ten rules of the type system
text:
5.3 Ten rules of the type system
Keep this table close for the first few weeks. Most of the confusion in this unit comes from one of these ten lines.








TypeScript




Type compatibility
structural – the shape decides, not the name (“duck typing”)


Types at runtime
none – they are erased during transpilation


Type inference
works almost everywhere; write types only where they help


“no value”
null and undefined – prefer undefined


Untyped escape hatch
any (avoid it) and unknown (the safe one)


One of several fixed values
a union of literal types: "a" | "b"


Operator overloading
does not exist – write compareTo, equals, …


Constants in a class
only static readonly


Generics at runtime
erased, like all other types


What is checked, and when
the compiler checks; the running program is plain JavaScript



The two lines to remember: structural typing and no types at runtime.

title: 5  Introduction to TypeScript
5  Introduction to TypeScript
5  Introduction to TypeScript
5  Introduction to TypeScript
text:
5.7 strict mode
The @tsconfig/next base configuration enables strict. The two rules that will bite you:

strictNullChecks – a string can never be null or undefined. If a value may be absent, say so: string | undefined.
noImplicitAny – a parameter without a type annotation is an error.

Do not turn these off. They are the reason for using TypeScript in the first place.

title: 5  Introduction to TypeScript
text:
5.8 Toolchain







Tool
Purpose




tsc
the TypeScript compiler: .ts → .js


tsx
runs a .ts file directly, without a visible compile step


tsconfig.json
compiler settings (target, module system, strictness, paths)


vitest
unit tests written in TypeScript



In this unit we run everything with tsx and never call tsc by hand. We set a project up together in class — the steps are in the first exercise.

⚠️ tsx only transpiles, it does not type-check. Your editor and npx tsc --noEmit do that. A program that runs is not necessarily a program that compiles.

title: 6  Arrays and Functions
text:
6.1 Arrays
Arrays and functions are the two things you will touch in every program from here on. The concepts will look familiar; the notation will not. And there is one habit to unlearn: in TypeScript you work on arrays with methods, not with loops. Anything you would write as a loop with an if inside has a shorter, clearer form here.
Arrays are not fixed size and not typed at runtime:
const protects the binding, not the contents. You cannot point the name at a different array, but you can still change the array it points at:

title: 6  Arrays and Functions
6  Arrays and Functions
6  Arrays and Functions
text:
6.3 The array methods
Three methods do most of the work. They differ in how many elements come out:



filter keeps some elements, map turns every element into a new one, reduce produces a single value


The rest of the table is variations on those three. All of these methods take a function as an argument (higher-order functions) and none of them modify the original array — they return a new one.








You want
TypeScript
Result




keep only some elements
filter(x => …)
fewer elements, same type


turn every element into something else
map(x => …)
same count, different type


boil the array down to one value
reduce(…)
a single value


find out whether any element fits
some(x => …)
boolean


find out whether all elements fit
every(x => …)
boolean


get the first matching element
find(x => …)
element or undefined


count the matching elements
filter(x => …).length
number


sort
toSorted((a, b) => …)
a sorted copy


sum
reduce((sum, x) => sum + x, 0)
number


copy the array
[...source]
a new array


index the elements by a key
new Map(source.map(x => [key, x]))
Map<K, V>


group the elements by a key
reduce into a Map (see below)
Map<K, V[]>



The three that matter most are filter, map and reduce. Almost everything else is a special case of one of them.
const readings = [
  { sensor: "outdoor", value: 21.5 },
  { sensor: "indoor", value: 23.1 },
  { sensor: "outdoor", value: 19.8 },
];

const outdoor = readings.filter((r) => r.sensor === "outdoor");
const values = readings.map((r) => r.value);
const total = values.reduce((sum, v) => sum + v, 0);
const average = total / values.length;
const warmest = readings.toSorted((a, b) => b.value - a.value)[0];
Note what find does when nothing matches: it returns undefined rather than throwing, and strict mode then forces you to handle that case before you can use the value.

6.3.1 Sorting
sort compares as strings by default — [10, 9, 1].sort() gives [1, 10, 9]. Always pass a comparator:
numbers.toSorted((a, b) => a - b);                      // ascending numbers
people.toSorted((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name)); // by name
toSorted returns a copy; the older sort sorts in place. Prefer toSorted, and the same for toReversed.


6.3.2 Grouping with Map
There is no ready-made method for grouping. The idiom is a reduce that builds up a Map, where each key holds the array of everything that belongs to it:
const bySensor = readings.reduce((map, r) => {
  const group = map.get(r.sensor) ?? [];
  group.push(r);
  return map.set(r.sensor, group);
}, new Map<string, typeof readings>());
A Map stores key/value pairs: get, set, has, delete, size, and it is iterable with for (const [key, value] of map). Prefer it over a plain object whenever the keys are data rather than fixed property names.


6.3.3 Chaining
const report = readings
  .filter((r) => r.value > 20)
  .map((r) => `${r.sensor}: ${r.value.toFixed(1)} °C`)
  .join(", ");
Each step produces a new array. That is fine for the data sizes in this unit and much easier to read than a loop.

title: 6  Arrays and Functions
text:
6.4 Loops
Still available where they are genuinely clearer:
for (const name of names) { … }          // the VALUES - this is the one you want
for (const key in someObject) { … }      // the KEYS - rarely what you want
names.forEach((name, index) => { … });   // no break, no return
Use for…of. Use for…in almost never.

title: 6  Arrays and Functions
text:
6.5 Two operators worth knowing
const port = config.port ?? 3000;        // null/undefined coalescing
const city = user?.address?.city;        // optional chaining -> undefined instead of a crash
?? reacts only to null and undefined, unlike || which also reacts to 0 and "" — a classic source of bugs.

title: 7  Asynchronous Programming and Files
text:
7.1 Node.js is single-threaded
Reading a file, calling a web service or querying a database takes time. This chapter is about what your program does in the meantime — and about the two keywords, async and await, that make waiting readable.
Node.js runs your JavaScript on a single thread. There is no second thread picking up work in the background.
That sounds like a limitation, and for calculation-heavy work it is. But a web server does almost no calculation: it waits — for the disk, the database, another web service. While one request waits, the single thread is free to serve the next one. This is why Node.js is fast for I/O-bound servers and a bad choice for CPU-bound work.
The consequence: never block the thread. A blocking call does not slow down one request, it freezes the whole server for everyone.
We use fs/promises exclusively in this unit.

8  HTTP, REST and Express
text:
8.1 HTTP in three minutes
You have used HTTP from the browser side for years. This chapter is about the other end: what a request actually contains, and how to answer one with Express.
We build the server step by step, and test every step with the REST Client before adding the next one. One route that you have really called beats four routes that you have not.
A client sends a request, a server sends back a response. Both consist of a start line, headers and an optional body.

title: 8  HTTP, REST and Express
text:
8.2 REST
A resource is a thing your API is about: an act, a tool, a loan. REST says: put the resource in the path (a noun, plural), and the verb in the HTTP method.
GET    /api/acts            all acts
GET    /api/acts/a1         one act
POST   /api/acts            create one
PUT    /api/acts/a1         replace one
DELETE /api/acts/a1         delete one

GET    /api/tools/t1/loans  the loans of one tool  (nested resource)
Not REST — the verb belongs in the method, not the path:
GET /api/getAllActs         no
GET /api/acts/delete/a1     no
POST /api/createAct         no

8.2.1 Three ways to pass data









Looks like
Use for




Route parameter
/api/acts/:id
which resource — required, part of the identity


Query parameter
/api/acts?stage=main&sort=time
filtering, sorting, paging — optional


Body
JSON in the request body
the data of the resource, for POST/PUT/PATCH

text:
8.6 Architecture: router and service
request  →  router  →  service  →  data (file, later: database)

The router speaks HTTP: read parameters, validate input, choose the status code. It contains no business logic.
The service contains the business logic and loads/stores the data. It knows nothing about HTTP — no Request, no Response, no status codes.

That separation is what makes the database unit possible: there you replace the data access inside the service with SQLite, and the router does not change at all.

title: 9  Objects, Types and Classes
text:
9.1 Object literals
You have met classes, inheritance and interfaces before. This chapter is about the parts TypeScript does its own way — and about when a class is the wrong tool and a plain type is the right one.
In JavaScript an object is created without a class. It is a bag of key/value pairs:
TypeScript infers the type of act from the literal. You can also name that type:
This is the workhorse of the unit. Most “objects” in our APIs are plain data with a type — no class needed.

title: 9  Objects, Types and Classes
9  Objects, Types and Classes
9  Objects, Types and Classes
text:
9.3 type or interface?
Both describe a shape, and for objects they are nearly interchangeable.




type
interface




Objects
yes
yes


Unions ("a" \| "b")
yes
no


Tuples, function types
yes
awkward


Can be re-opened / merged
no
yes


extends
via &
yes



Convention for this unit: use type everywhere. Use interface only when you really want a contract that several classes implement. Do not prefix interface names with I; TypeScript does not do that.

title: 9  Objects, Types and Classes
9  Objects, Types and Classes
text:
9.5 Classes vs. plain objects







Use a class when
Use a type when




there is behaviour, not just data
it is pure data


there are invariants to protect
it comes from JSON or goes into JSON


you need instanceof
you need a DTO



Remember from 03_async-and-files:
const tools = JSON.parse(text) as Tool[]; // NOT Tool instances - no methods!
JSON.parse produces plain objects. as Tool[] only silences the compiler; calling a method on one of them crashes at runtime. If you want real instances, construct them:
const tools = (JSON.parse(text) as ToolDto[]).map((dto) => Tool.fromDto(dto));
This is the toDto/fromDto pattern, and it is the heart of EX4.

title: 9  Objects, Types and Classes
9  Objects, Types and Classes
text:
9.7 Equality
"1" == 1; // true  - == converts types. Never use it.
"1" === 1; // false - === compares type and value. Always use this.

({ a: 1 } === { a: 1 }); // false - reference comparison
There is no operator overloading, and no built-in convention for value equality. If you need it, write an equals method and call it explicitly.

title: 10  SQLite
text:
10.1 Why SQLite
Until now our data lived in files that we read completely into memory and wrote back completely on every change. That works for a dozen records. It does not work for a real application:
A database solves all three. From DBI you already know relational databases and SQL; this unit is about using one from Node.js. We use SQLite.
SQLite is not a server. It is a file plus a library that reads and writes it, and the library runs inside your own process. There is nothing to install, nothing to configure, no port and no password.
SQLite is the most widely deployed database in the world: every phone in the room contains several, and many programs store their settings or save games in a SQLite file. It is also faster and more capable than its reputation; the SQLite team’s own guide considers it fine for websites with up to about 100,000 visits a day. Its one real limit is the single writer: many connections can read at the same time, but only one can write. It fits applications that read a lot and write a little, which describes most of our exercises.

title: 10  SQLite

title: 10  SQLite
text:
10.2 The driver: node:sqlite
Node.js ships SQLite built in as the module node:sqlite. There is no npm install and nothing is compiled on your machine:
import { DatabaseSync } from "node:sqlite";

const db = new DatabaseSync("data/library.db"); // creates the file if it does not exist
Older projects use the packages better-sqlite3 or sqlite3. They work in a similar way, but they are extra dependencies with a native part that has to be built or downloaded during npm install, which is exactly what the built-in module avoids.

10.2.1 Database access is IO, and IO is asynchronous
A database is IO, just like reading a file or calling another server over the network. The chapter on asynchronous programming explained why IO must not block the single thread of Node.js, and for almost every database that is the rule: the driver sends the query to a database server and returns a Promise, and you await the result.
node:sqlite is the exception, and DatabaseSync says so in its name: every call blocks until it is finished. That is acceptable here for one reason only. SQLite runs inside our own process and works on a local file, so there is no network in between and a query takes microseconds, and the API becomes much simpler.
So from now on our services are synchronous: they return values, not Promises. Only explicit file access, for example reading a CSV file for an import, stays async. Keep in mind that this is a special case. With any database server you will be back to async and await.

title: 10  SQLite
text:
10.3 Creating a schema
The tables are created with plain SQL. We keep the statements in a file data/schema.sql and execute it with db.exec(...), which runs several statements at once:
CREATE TABLE books (
  isbn   TEXT    NOT NULL,
  title  TEXT    NOT NULL,
  author TEXT    NOT NULL,
  year   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT pk_books PRIMARY KEY (isbn)
) STRICT;

CREATE TABLE loans (
  id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  isbn    TEXT    NOT NULL,
  student TEXT    NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT pk_loans PRIMARY KEY (id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_loans_book FOREIGN KEY (isbn) REFERENCES books (isbn)
) STRICT;

Name your constraints (pk_books, fk_loans_book). When one is violated, the name tells you which rule was broken.
Order matters: loans refers to books, so books has to exist first, and when you drop the tables it is the other way round.
An INTEGER primary key gets its value from the database when you insert a row without it. That is how loans.id is filled.


10.3.1 Types and STRICT
SQLite has only a handful of types:







Type
Used for




INTEGER
whole numbers, and booleans as 0 / 1


REAL
floating point numbers


TEXT
strings, and dates as ISO strings (2026-11-24, 2026-11-24T10:15:00)


BLOB
binary data, rarely needed



There is no date type and no boolean type. ISO dates are a good choice anyway: they sort correctly as strings, and SQLite’s date functions understand them.
Without STRICT, SQLite stores whatever you give it: 'abc' ends up in an INTEGER column without an error. STRICT at the end of CREATE TABLE switches that off, and the database then refuses values of the wrong type. We always use it.


10.3.2 Foreign keys: it depends on who opens the file
Three things the database now guarantees, which no amount of TypeScript could:

PRIMARY KEY: no two books with the same ISBN.
CHECK (...): a rule for the values of a column, for example CONSTRAINT ck_books_year CHECK (year > 0). It is the runtime counterpart of a union type.
FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES: a loan cannot point at a book that does not exist.


⚠️ SQLite itself does not enforce foreign keys by default, for historic reasons. Whether they are enforced depends on the program that opens the database: node:sqlite switches them on for every connection it opens, but the sqlite3 command line tool, many database viewers and other drivers do not. There, every connection has to switch them on itself:
db.exec("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON");
We do not need this line, because node:sqlite already does it. If you ever use a different driver or tool and suddenly can insert a loan for a book that does not exist, this is why.

section: 10.7 The database file is not committed
text:
10.7 The database file is not committed
Do not commit the .db file. Put *.db into .gitignore and commit two things instead: the schema (data/schema.sql) and a seed script (npm run seed) that creates the database from scratch and fills it with sample data. Then anyone can recreate the database at any time, and you can always go back to a clean state.

⚠️ On Windows, a running server keeps the .db file open. Stop the server before you delete the file or run the seed script again.

title: 11  Queries
text:
11.1 SQL injection
You know SELECT, joins and GROUP BY from DBI. This chapter is about running such queries from TypeScript safely, and about turning what comes back into something an API can return. All examples use the database of a small parking garage:
Imagine a login that checks the user name and password like this:
A user who types x' OR '1'='1 as the password turns the statement into
AND binds stronger than OR, so the condition is true for every row, and the attacker is logged in without knowing any password. With other input they can read other tables, change data or delete it (the classic comic). This is SQL injection, and it is still one of the most common security holes in web applications.
The cause is always the same: a value from the outside became part of the SQL text. The fix is always the same as well: a prepared statement with placeholders.
The statement is compiled first, and the values are passed separately. Whatever the user types is compared as a string and can never change the structure of the statement.

text:
11.6 Joins
An inner join returns only rows that have a partner on both sides:
SELECT p.arrived, p.departed, p.fee, s.floor, s.number
  FROM parkings p
  JOIN spots s ON s.id = p.spot_id
 WHERE p.license_plate = ?
 ORDER BY p.arrived DESC
A left (outer) join keeps every row of the left table, and fills the columns of the right table with NULL where there is no partner. That is what you need for “all floors, and how many cars are on each”, including floors that are empty:
SELECT s.floor, COUNT(*) AS totalSpots, COUNT(p.id) AS occupied
  FROM spots s
  LEFT JOIN parkings p ON p.spot_id = s.id AND p.departed IS NULL
 GROUP BY s.floor

⚠️ ON or WHERE? The condition p.departed IS NULL is part of the join here: “join only the parkings that are still running”. Moved into a WHERE, it is applied after the join. A spot whose cars have all left joins only rows with a departed date, the WHERE removes them all, and the spot disappears from the result. totalSpots is then wrong. Rule of thumb: conditions on the right table of a LEFT JOIN go into ON.

A table can also be joined with itself, for example employees with their manager, who is another employee. Give the table two aliases, and use a LEFT JOIN so the boss, who has no manager, is not lost.

title: 11  Queries
text:
11.7 Grouping and aggregates







Function
Result




COUNT(*)
number of rows in the group


COUNT(column)
number of rows where column is not NULL


COUNT(DISTINCT column)
number of different values


SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
as the name says; NULL if there were no values


ROUND(x, 2)
rounded to 2 decimal places


COALESCE(x, 0)
x, or 0 if x is NULL



In the occupancy query above, COUNT(*) counts all spots of a floor, while COUNT(p.id) counts only those that found a current parking. The outer join produced NULL for the others.
WHERE filters rows before they are grouped, HAVING filters groups afterwards:
SELECT c.owner, COUNT(*) AS parkings
  FROM cars c
  JOIN parkings p ON p.license_plate = c.license_plate
 WHERE p.departed IS NOT NULL      -- only finished parkings
 GROUP BY c.owner
HAVING COUNT(*) >= ?              -- only regular customers
 ORDER BY parkings DESC

⚠️ Joining two “many” sides at once multiplies rows. If a floor has 8 spots and you join both the spots and all past parkings, every spot appears once per parking, and COUNT(*) no longer counts spots. COUNT(DISTINCT s.id) counts them correctly again, or you compute one of the numbers in a subquery.

An aggregate without GROUP BY returns exactly one row. SUM over no rows is NULL, not 0, so a revenue query for a day without any parking needs COALESCE(SUM(fee), 0).

title: 11  Queries
text:
11.8 Subqueries
A query inside a query. The most useful forms for us:
-- cars that have never parked
SELECT * FROM cars c
 WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM parkings p WHERE p.license_plate = c.license_plate);

-- spots on the floor with the most electric spots
SELECT * FROM spots
 WHERE floor = (SELECT floor FROM spots WHERE kind = 'electric'
                 GROUP BY floor ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1);
EXISTS / NOT EXISTS asks “is there at least one matching row?” and is often the clearest way to write a condition about another table. A subquery in = must return exactly one value.

title: 11  Queries
text:
11.9 Dates
SQLite stores dates as TEXT, and its date functions work on ISO strings:







Expression
Result




date('2026-11-24 14:30:00')
'2026-11-24'


strftime('%Y', arrived)
the year as text, '2026'


date('now')
today (in UTC)


julianday(departed) - julianday(arrived)
the difference in days, as a decimal number



Because ISO strings sort correctly, you can compare them directly. Be careful with ranges: departed <= '2026-11-30' misses '2026-11-30 17:00:00', because the longer string is “greater”. Compare the date part instead:
SELECT date(departed) AS day, COUNT(*) AS parkings, ROUND(SUM(fee), 2) AS revenue
  FROM parkings
 WHERE date(departed) BETWEEN ? AND ?   -- inclusive on both ends
 GROUP BY date(departed)
 ORDER BY day

12  Writing and Transactions
text:
12.1 Inserting
Reading data is half of an API. This chapter is about the other half: creating, changing and deleting rows, answering with the right status code, and making sure that an operation made of several statements happens completely or not at all. The examples use the parking garage from the previous chapter.
Tables with an INTEGER primary key get their id from the database when you leave the column out. run reports it as id (the driver calls it lastInsertRowid), so you can return it to the client.
A successful POST answers 201 Created with the new resource in the body and its address in the Location header:

title: 12  Writing and Transactions
12  Writing and Transactions
text:
12.2 Updating and deleting
UPDATE and DELETE do not fail when no row matches. They just change nothing, and changes is 0. That is how you find out whether the resource existed:
const result = this.unit.run("DELETE FROM cars WHERE license_plate = :plate", { plate });
return result.changes === 1 ? "deleted" : "not-found";
A condition in the UPDATE can do part of the checking for you. A car can leave only once:
UPDATE parkings SET departed = :departed, fee = :fee
 WHERE id = :id AND departed IS NULL
changes === 0 now means “unknown id” or “already left”. One SELECT tells the two apart: 404 Not Found or 409 Conflict.

12.2.1 Deleting rows that others refer to
If parkings refer to a car, the foreign key decides what happens when the car is deleted:







Foreign key
Deleting the car …




REFERENCES cars (license_plate)
fails with “FOREIGN KEY constraint failed”


... ON DELETE CASCADE
deletes its parkings as well


... ON DELETE SET NULL
keeps the parkings, the column becomes NULL (it must be nullable)



Which one is right is a decision about the domain, not about SQL. For the garage, the history of a car that is removed from the system can go, so fk_parkings_car uses ON DELETE CASCADE. A car that is parked right now must not be deleted at all. That is a rule the service checks before deleting, and it answers 409.

title: 12  Writing and Transactions
text:
12.3 Insert or update: ON CONFLICT
PUT /api/cars/L-777XY means “this car should look like this”, whether it exists or not. SQLite can do both in one statement, an upsert:
INSERT INTO cars (license_plate, model, owner) VALUES (:plate, :model, :owner)
ON CONFLICT (license_plate) DO UPDATE SET model = excluded.model, owner = excluded.owner
excluded is the row that could not be inserted. Whether the car was new (201) or updated (200) is not visible in the result, so the service checks with a SELECT first, inside the same transaction.

title: 12  Writing and Transactions
12  Writing and Transactions
12  Writing and Transactions
text:
12.6 Transactions
From DBI you know what a transaction guarantees: atomicity (all or nothing), consistency (constraints hold afterwards), isolation (others do not see half-finished work) and durability (committed is committed).
db.exec("BEGIN");
// ... several statements ...
db.exec("COMMIT"); // or ROLLBACK to undo everything since BEGIN

12.6.1 Every statement is atomic on its own
Without BEGIN, SQLite runs each statement in its own small transaction (autocommit). An UPDATE that changes ten rows changes all ten or none. So a single INSERT does not need a transaction. You need one as soon as several statements belong together:







Situation
Transaction?




A request only reads
no


A request runs exactly one writing statement
not strictly, but we start one anyway, see below


A request writes several rows or tables that belong together
yes


A request checks something and then writes based on the result (check-then-act)
yes





12.6.2 Check-then-act
When a car arrives, the service checks that the spot is free and the car is not parked elsewhere, and then inserts the parking. Two things can go wrong without a transaction:

Half-finished work. If something fails after the first of several writes, the first one stays in the database. With a transaction, the rollback removes it.
Someone else changes the data between the check and the write. Our handlers are synchronous, and Node runs one at a time, so inside our own server two requests cannot interleave there today. That changes as soon as there is an await between check and write, or another process writes to the same database file: a second instance of the server, an import script, a person in a database tool. Then two cars can be checked into the same free spot.

A transaction makes the check and the write one unit. In SQLite only one connection can write at a time, and while our transaction holds the write lock, nobody else can change what we just checked.


12.6.3 Isolation in SQLite
SQLite transactions are serializable, the strictest level: there is only one writer at a time, and nobody sees changes that are not committed. A plain BEGIN is deferred: it takes the write lock only at the first writing statement. If another connection is writing at that moment, a transaction that already read something can fail halfway with “database is locked”. BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the write lock at the start, so a transaction either cannot start or runs to the end. We always use it for writing.

title: 12  Writing and Transactions
12  Writing and Transactions
section: 12.8 One connection here, a pool elsewhere
text:
12.8 One connection here, a pool elsewhere
Our application keeps one connection open for its whole life. That fits SQLite: the driver is synchronous, there is only one writer anyway, and the transaction rules above keep requests apart. A database server is different. There, a request waits for the network, many requests run at the same time, and each transaction needs a connection of its own. Applications then keep a pool of connections and hand one to each request.

title: 13  Testing and Importing
text:
13.1 Unit tests and integration tests
The last two topics of the unit belong together: tests tell you that your services do what they should, and an import is the classic piece of code that you would never trust without them. The examples use the parking garage again.
You know vitest from unit 02. With a database, there are two kinds of tests:
Write as much as possible as pure functions (input in, result out, no database, no clock): they are the easiest to test. Everything else is tested through the services. We do not test the routers with automated tests; requests.http covers them.
